messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: There was no difference in depressive symptom scores (CES-D) between the 50,000 IU and 5,000 IU vitamin D3 dose groups.
Sentence: "There was no difference in CES-D scores by treatment dose."
Measured as: CES-D scores
Population: Women with type 2 diabetes, significant depressive symptoms (CES-D) and low vitamin D
Intervention: Vitamin D3 50,000 IU weekly orally for 6 months
Comparator: Active comparator vitamin D3 5,000 IU weekly
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 129
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Winter light therapy reduced depression scores in adolescents.
Sentence: "Winter light therapy increases vitamin D (Δ = 8.2 ng/mL, p < 0.001) and reduces depression (ΔPHQ-9=-3.1, p = 0.005)."
Measured as: depression (PHQ-9)
Population: Chinese adolescents in winter RCTs (N = 200)
Intervention: Winter light therapy
Comparator: Not reported
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 7,321
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Study B's exposure is light therapy, not vitamin D supplementation (vitamin D rises only as a by-product), so it is not a vitamin D comparison.","verdict":"off_question","reason":null,"also_differs":[],"detail":"exposure: winter light therapy (not vitamin D)"}
